headline: With every lane on its own best practice the field converges near 1.6M renders/s, and next-yak's automatic CSS-variable path costs 2.08× against the inline style the other lanes write by hand.

microbench.why: Lanes without native dynamic-value support split the static class from the moving value by hand, and it works: `cnfast` reaches 1.62M renders/s from 574,000 on the naive pattern, `panda` 1.00M from 222,000, `goober` 945,000 from 166,000. `next-yak-css` sits with them at 1.54M without anyone writing that split, because the compiler performs it. The styled lane takes a different route and pays for it: `next-yak` at 724,000 passes the value through a CSS custom property on a wrapper, 0.783 ms of lib self-time against 0.000 ms for the css prop. The convergence is real, and so is what reaching it costs — a manual optimization repeated for every dynamic value in the codebase.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css` at 1,347 req/s leads. The hand-written split rescues the runtime lanes under load as well: `styled-components` reaches 561 req/s against 186 on the naive pattern, and `goober` 674 against 152.

attribution.why: `next-yak-css` at 0.756 ms and `bamboo` at 0.762 ms hold the floor. `next-yak` at 1.34 ms is the slowest compile-time lane in the case, and what it pays for is the custom-property wrapper rather than any per-instance serialization. `emotion` at 2.46 ms stays the ceiling even with the hand-written split applied.

hydrate.why: The naive pattern's hydration cliff disappears: `goober` needs 81.0 ms here against 1,265 ms on `dyn-translate`. Eight lanes finish between 46.5 ms and 49.9 ms.

inp.why: Fourteen lanes answer between 6.5 ms and 7.8 ms, flat at this spread. Changing a value on one element is cheap however the value is authored.

mount.why: `next-yak-css` at 60.0 ms leads a band running to 76.3 ms for twelve lanes. `goober` mounts in 79.2 ms against 1,241 ms on the naive pattern, the same rescue hydration shows.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane, 0.106 ms to 0.171 ms. Moving the value out of the selector holds the engine's matching work constant.

payload.why: `vanilla` at 5,502 gz B is the floor and the compile-time lanes sit just above it. The hand-written split fixes the wire too: `emotion` ships 18.4 kB here against 39.4 kB on the naive pattern and `styled-components` 18.9 kB against 35.5 kB, because one static rule replaces a thousand unique ones.

nsweep.why: `next-yak-css` at 2.58 ms and `vanilla` at 2.70 ms hold a flat line to the largest size, with the utility lanes joining at 2.71 ms and 2.79 ms. `next-yak` at 5.30 ms carries its custom-property cost as a slope, and `emotion` at 9.63 ms stays the steepest.

crossCase: The trio reads as one argument. The Example `dyn-translate` shown above is the naive pattern, what a codebase produces when nobody optimizes: `goober` at 166,000 renders/s and a 1.27 s hydration. This case is every lane at its best, and for a library without native support that best is hand-written, the developer splitting static class from inline style per component, for every dynamic value, indefinitely. next-yak ships that separation as a compiler feature instead. The Example `dyn-inline` shown below removes the last variable by putting every lane, next-yak included, on a plain inline style, and `next-yak` renders 1.51M there against 724,000 here, which prices its CSS-variable path at 2.08×.
